content: Léon Charles Albert Calmette, born on July 12, 1863, in Nice, France, was a French physician, bacteriologist, and immunologist who played a pivotal role in the development of modern medicine. He is best known for his discovery of Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), an attenuated strain of Mycobacterium used in the BCG vaccine to prevent tuberculosis. Additionally, he developed the first antivenin for snake venom, known as Calmette's serum. Calmette initially aspired to serve in the Navy as a physician and joined the School of Naval Physicians in Brest in 1881. By 1883, he began his service in the Naval Medical Corps in Hong Kong, where he conducted research on malaria and earned his doctoral degree in 1886. Subsequently, he was stationed in Saint-Pierre and Miquelon in 1887 and later served in West Africa, including Gabon and French Congo, where he studied diseases such as malaria, sleeping sickness, and pellagra. Upon returning to France in 1890, Calmette met Louis Pasteur and Emile Roux, who became his mentors. Under Pasteur's guidance, he was tasked with establishing and directing a branch of the Pasteur Institute in Saigon (French Indochina) in 1891. There, he delved into toxicology, studying venoms from snakes and bees, as well as plant toxins like curare. He also organized the production of vaccines for smallpox and rabies and conducted research on cholera and the fermentation of opium and rice. In 1894, Calmette returned to France and developed the first antivenoms for snake bites using immune sera derived from vaccinated horses. This innovation, known as Calmette's serum, laid the groundwork for further advancements in antivenom production by other researchers, such as Vital Brazil in Brazil. Calmette also collaborated with Alexandre Yersin, the discoverer of Yersinia pestis, to create the first immune serum against the bubonic plague. He traveled to Portugal to assist in combating a plague epidemic in Oporto. In 1895, Emile Roux appointed Calmette as the director of the Pasteur Institute's branch in Lille, where he worked for 25 years. During his tenure, he founded the first antituberculosis dispensary in Lille in 1901, naming it after Emile Roux. In 1904, he established the Ligue du Nord contre la Tuberculose (Northern Antituberculosis League), which continues to operate today. In 1909, he contributed to the establishment of a Pasteur Institute branch in Algiers, and in 1918, he became the assistant director of the Pasteur Institute in Paris. Calmette's most significant scientific achievement was his work on developing a vaccine against tuberculosis, a disease that was a leading cause of death at the time. Building on Robert Koch's 1882 discovery of Mycobacterium tuberculosis as the causative agent of tuberculosis, Calmette collaborated with veterinarian and immunologist Camille Guérin. Guérin had demonstrated that immunity to tuberculosis was linked to the presence of live tubercle bacilli in the bloodstream. Using Pasteur's principles, Calmette and Guérin developed an attenuated strain of bovine tubercle bacilli by cultivating them in a bile-containing medium, an idea inspired by Norwegian researcher Kristian Feyer Andvord. From 1908 to 1921, Calmette and Guérin worked to produce progressively less virulent strains of the bacillus through successive cultures. In 1921, they successfully used the BCG vaccine to immunize newborns at the Charité hospital in Paris. However, the vaccination program faced a major setback in 1930 when 72 children in Lübeck, Germany, developed tuberculosis due to contamination of vaccine batches. This incident temporarily halted mass vaccination programs, which were only reinstated in 1932 after the implementation of safer production methods. The Lübeck tragedy profoundly affected Calmette, and he passed away in Paris on October 29, 1933, one year after the incident. He was the brother of Gaston Calmette, the editor of Le Figaro, who was murdered in 1914 by Henriette Caillaux, the wife of Finance Minister Joseph Caillaux.
